lesson.title: Measuring turns

lead.text: Stand in the middle of a room and face a door. Turn until you face that door again and you have made a whole turn. Turn only until you face the opposite wall and you have made half of one, a half-turn. Stop when you face the wall on your left or right and you have made a quarter-turn.

These turns fit together neatly. Two quarter-turns make a half-turn, and four make a whole turn, whichever way you are facing when you start. Turns can also be added like lengths. A half-turn followed by another half-turn is a whole turn, and you are facing the door again.

Counting in quarter-turns is enough for the skater at the start of the lesson. It is too coarse for most jobs, though. A door that has swung open a little has made neither a quarter-turn nor a half-turn, and to describe that you need a scale with finer marks. First, the skater's problem.

diagram.alt: A person seen from above in the middle of a room, with a door in the top wall. Three views show a quarter-turn, a half-turn and a whole turn, each as an arc from the door direction to the way the person faces.
diagram.caption: The dashed line points at the door. The curved arrow shows the turn and the solid line shows where the person ends up facing. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Use the quarter-turn as your unit and count what she has made.

A finer scale cuts the whole turn into 360 equal small turns. Each one is called a degree and is written 1°, so a whole turn is 360° and a half-turn is half of that. The number 360 was chosen long ago because it divides evenly in so many ways, which lets you cut a turn into halves, quarters, fifths and many other equal parts.

Two straight lines that meet at a point leave a gap between them, and the size of that gap is an angle. The corner of this page is an angle, and so is the gap between the hands of a clock. We measure an angle by how much turning it takes to swing one line round onto the other, using degrees.
The corner of a page is a quarter of a whole turn. An angle like that is called a right angle. You already have what you need to find its size in degrees.

diagram.alt: A circle with a shaded wedge measured from a flat arm. The four views show a wedge of 1 degree, a right angle of 90 degrees, a half-turn of 180 degrees and a whole turn of 360 degrees, all drawn to scale.
diagram.caption: Each wedge is drawn to scale, measured round from the horizontal arm. Use the buttons to compare the sizes.

lead.text: Use the size of a whole turn and the fraction of it that a right angle takes up.

A right angle measures 90°. Now cut one in two. Draw a line from the corner of a page out across the page, and the single right angle becomes two smaller angles side by side. Together they fill the corner exactly as before, so their sizes must add up to 90°.

That gives a way to find a missing angle with one subtraction. If you know the whole and one part, the other part is what remains. Say one part is 25°. The other is 90° − 25° = 65°. The figure shows two corners, each with one part marked. Switch between them and see how the leftover part changes.

afterFigure.text: The same reasoning works wherever a fixed amount of turn is shared between pieces. A corner is only the first case, with a total of 90°. The next case has a bigger total.

lead.text: Here is a corner with one part marked. The other part is the rest of the corner.

Turn through a half-turn and you finish facing the opposite way, so a half-turn is what a straight line looks like when you draw it. Its size is 180°. An angle of exactly that size is called a straight angle. Now split a straight angle by drawing a line out from a point on it. You get two angles side by side, and together they fill the straight line.

The idea from the corner carries over with a new total. Two angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so each one is 180° minus the other. If one is 120°, the other is 180° − 120° = 60°. The answer is smaller than the total, which makes a quick check: a part is never bigger than the whole it came from.

afterFigure.text: A straight line is half a turn. That leaves the other half still to come, and the full circle is the last case.

lead.text: Two angles share a straight line, and you know one of them.

steps.headline: All the way round a point

lead.text: Stand where several lines meet and look round you. The angles between neighbouring lines go all the way round the point and fill the whole turn. A whole turn is 360°, so the angles round a point add up to 360°.

The total also tells you how much turn is left on a dial. A pointer that has swung through 200° has 360° − 200° = 160° of its turn still to come. The figure shows the part already made and the part that remains. Together they fill the circle.
Every problem so far has worked the same way. Decide which total applies, 90° in a corner, 180° on a line or 360° round a point, then take away the parts you know.
A pointer sweeps round a dial, and part of its turn is already made.

One more point about angles before the check. Compare the minute hand of a clock on a church tower with the minute hand of a wristwatch. From 12 to 3 each hand turns through a right angle, although one is a metre long and the other a few millimetres.
The two lines that make an angle are called its arms. Drawing the arms longer makes the picture bigger and adds no turn, because the turn depends only on the directions the arms point.

So the size of an angle never depends on how long its arms are. That matters when you read a diagram, where a long arm can make one angle look larger than another even when the two match. The figure shows two right angles with arms of different lengths.

diagram.alt: Two angles side by side. One has long arms and one has short arms, and both are right angles of 90 degrees.
diagram.caption: Both angles are 90°. Only the direction of the arms sets the turn, so the longer arms add nothing.

lesson.orientation: Use quarter, half and full turns to find an unknown angle.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A skater glides onto the ice, faces the far end of the rink and spins on the spot. She makes half a turn, so she is looking back at the way she came in. Then she spins on for one more quarter-turn and stops.

She wants to finish facing the far end, as she did when she began, but she isn't sure how much further to spin. A coach at the barrier can tell her at once by counting how much of a turn she has made and how much is left.

Almost every shape has corners, and a corner is a turn. This lesson starts with the skater. It gives you a way to put a number on a turn, and then a quick way to find the missing part of a turn whenever the rest is known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure turns in degrees and find a missing angle in a corner, on a line and round a point.

recap.keyIdea: An angle measures a turn. Angles that fill a corner add to 90°, so a missing one is found by subtraction. A straight line and a full turn work the same way, with totals of 180° and 360°.

blocks.text: Back with the skater, you counted the quarter-turns she had made and found the one still to come. After that you put numbers on turns, and found a missing part each time by subtracting what you knew from the total.
You found 112° beside 68° on a line and 220° left of a full turn after 140°, and you saw that longer arms change nothing about the angle.

recap.nextHook: A straight line is a half-turn of 180°. Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and set them side by side, and they seem to fill that straight line exactly. The next lesson checks whether that always happens.

questions.prompt: A 90° corner contains a 35° angle. How many degrees remain?
hints: Identify the total turn of the corner.
Subtract the known part from the total.
Calculate 90 − 35.
questions.onCorrect: The two parts fill the corner, so they add to 90°. Take the part you know from the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: 35° is the part you were given. The question asks for the part that is left.
That adds the 35° to the corner. The two parts together make the corner, not more.

questions.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is 68°. What is the other, in degrees?
hints: A straight line represents a half-turn.
The adjacent angles add to 180°.
Calculate 180 − 68.
questions.onCorrect: The other angle is 180° − 68° = 112°: the two angles fill the half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: 68° is the angle you were given. Find the part that is left.
That adds 180 to 68. The whole is 180°, so the other part is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A pointer has turned 140°. How many more degrees complete a full 360° turn in the same direction?
hints: Use a full turn as the total.
Find the turn that has not yet been made.
Calculate 360 − 140.
questions.onCorrect: 220°. The turn so far and the turn left make a full 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 140° is the turn already made. Find the part still to come.
That is 180 − 140. A full turn is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: The arms of an angle are drawn twice as long, along the same lines. What happens to its size in degrees?
hints: Separate the length of a ray from its direction.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The degree measure depends on the directions of the rays, so extending them leaves the angle unchanged.

questions.onCorrect: The angle stays the same. It measures how far you turn, not how long the arms are.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer arm covers more paper, not more turn. The directions of the arms haven't changed.
Nothing was cut. The arms point the same way, so the turn is the same.

questions.prompt: A right angle is split into 27° and another angle. Find the other angle in degrees.
hints: A right angle is the whole.
Subtract the part already given.
Calculate 90 − 27.
questions.onCorrect: 63°. The parts of a right angle add to 90°, so subtract the part you know.

misconceptions.feedback: 117° comes from starting at 180°. A right angle is a quarter-turn, so start from 90°.
27° is the part you were given. Find the other part.

questions.prompt: Which pair of angles can sit side by side to form a straight angle?
hints: Add each pair and compare with a half-turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 72° + 108° = 180°, the measure of a straight angle.

questions.onCorrect: 72° + 108° = 180°. Two angles on a straight line fill a half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 90°, a right angle. A straight angle is a half-turn.
Those add to more than a half-turn: 190°.

questions.prompt: A skater makes a half-turn and then one more quarter-turn. How many more quarter-turns bring her back to facing the way she started?
hints: How many quarter-turns make one whole turn?
A half-turn is two quarter-turns. How many has she made so far?
Take the quarter-turns she has made from the number in a whole turn.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Half a turn is 2 quarter-turns, plus 1 more is 3. A whole turn is 4, so 1 more is needed.

questions.onCorrect: 1. A whole turn is 4 quarter-turns, and she has made 3. Angles measure how much of a turn has happened.

misconceptions.feedback: That's a whole turn from the start. She has already made some of it.
That's the half-turn she has made. Count the extra quarter-turn too.

questions.prompt: How many degrees is a right angle?
hints: A right angle is one quarter of a full turn.
How many degrees is a full turn?
Share 360° into four equal parts.
questions.onCorrect: 90°. A right angle is a quarter of 360°, the corner of a page.

misconceptions.feedback: 180° is a half-turn, a straight line. A right angle is half of that.
45° is an eighth of a turn. A right angle is a quarter.

questions.prompt: Why do the two angles add to 180°?
hints: What fraction of a turn is a straight line?

acceptedIdeas: Together they fill a half-turn, and a straight line is a half-turn.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Together they fill a half-turn, and a straight line is a half-turn.

choices.label: Together they fill a half-turn, and a straight line is a half-turn.
Every pair of angles adds to 180°.
Because 180° is the size of a right angle.

questions.onCorrect: Two angles on a straight line fill a half-turn, so they add to 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: Only angles that fill a straight line do. A corner's parts add to 90°.
A right angle is 90°. A straight line is twice that.

questions.prompt: Three angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn. Two of them are 100° and 150°. What is the third, in degrees?
hints: What is the total of all three angles round a point?
Add the two angles you know.
Take that sum from the total.
questions.onCorrect: 110°. Angles round a point fill a full turn, so they add to 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 250° is the two angles added together. The third angle is what is left of the turn.
That is 180 − 100. Round a point the total is 360°, not 180°.
